title: Florence to the Empyrean: the Exile, the Mountain, and the Rose
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Florence: the Boy and the Vision

stops.name: Florence, birth under Gemini
stops.campa: Dante is born in the sesto of San Piero Maggiore, in the shadow of the Badia, to Alighiero di Bellincione and Bella, minor Guelph nobility gone toward trade. He will later tell the sky itself which stars stood over the room: Gemini, the twins, the sign of wit and letters, whose light he says he draws all his genius from, such as it is. Within days he is carried to the ancient octagonal font of San Giovanni to be named and washed clean, the temple he will call, from exile, his beautiful San Giovanni, the one roof of Florence he is never allowed to see again.
stops.quote: O gloriose stelle, o lume pregno di gran virtù, dal quale io riconosco tutto, qual che si sia, il mio ingegno.
suggested_refs: The octagonal Battistero di San Giovanni, where Dante was baptized
sources: Boccaccio, Trattatello in laude di Dante

stops.name: Florence, the first sight of Beatrice
stops.campa: At a May Day gathering in the house of Folco Portinari, the two children not yet nine years old see each other for the first time. She wears a subdued, noble red, sashed and adorned as befits her young age, and from that hour, Dante will write, the spirit of life begins to tremble so violently in the most secret chamber of his heart that he feels it in his smallest pulses. He does not speak to her. He does not need to. He calls her, already, in his own mind, by a name that means she who blesses: Beatrice.
stops.quote: Apparve vestita di nobilissimo colore, umile e onesto, sanguigno, cinta e ornata a la guisa che a la sua giovanissima etade si convenia.
suggested_refs: The Portinari family loggia, near the Badia Fiorentina
Henry Holiday's 1883 painting Dante and Beatrice
sources: Boccaccio, Trattatello in laude di Dante

stops.name: Florence, the second greeting
stops.campa: Nine years to the season after the first sight, he meets her again on a Florentine street, now grown, dressed in purest white, walking between two older women. She turns and greets him with her voice, a courtesy so entire that he says he touches, in that moment, the outer edge of blessedness itself. He flees to his room to be alone with the feeling, and there, half sleeping, dreams the vision of Love holding his own burning heart out for her to eat. He will spend the rest of his life arguing with poets over what the dream meant.
suggested_refs: Dante Gabriel Rossetti's illustrations for the Vita Nuova

stops.name: Florence, the death of Beatrice
stops.campa: Beatrice, married some years now to the banker Simone de' Bardi, dies at twenty-four. Dante, who has never once named her Bardi and never will, works out afterward an entire numerology of the number nine to prove that a miracle, not a fever, has taken her: that she was herself a nine, a miracle whose only root is the Trinity. He falls first into ruinous grief, briefly into the arms of a donna gentile who almost consoles him, then closes the little book of her memory with a vow that will take him thirty years and three canticles to keep.
stops.quote: Io spero di dicer di lei quello che mai non fue detto d'alcuna.
suggested_refs: Beatrice's tomb, Chiesa di Santa Margherita de' Cerchi, Florence (traditional site)
sources: Boccaccio, Trattatello in laude di Dante

stops.name: Florence, marriage to Gemma Donati
stops.campa: Betrothed since childhood by a contract his father arranged, Dante marries Gemma di Manetto Donati, of the same great clan that will later produce both his fiercest political enemy, Corso Donati, and his own protector by marriage. She will bear him at least four children, Giovanni, Pietro, Jacopo, and Antonia, and will not follow him into exile. In the whole of his life's work, the Vita Nuova, the Convivio, the hundred cantos of the Commedia, he never once writes her name.
suggested_refs: The Donati family tower district, Florence
sources: Boccaccio, Trattatello in laude di Dante

stops.name: Campaldino, the cavalry charge
stops.campa: Twenty-four years old, Dante rides in the front rank of Florentine feditori against the Ghibellines of Arezzo on the plain below Poppi. The Aretine cavalry breaks the first Florentine line before the Guelph infantry and reserve turn the field; Buonconte da Montefeltro, the enemy commander, dies in the rout and is never found, his body claimed later, in another book, by a devil and an angel disputing over a single tear. Dante will write, in a letter no longer surviving but quoted by his first biographer, of the terror of a green soldier and the great joy that came after.
stops.quote: Io mi trovai non fanciullo nell'armi... ebbi temenza molta... e nella fine allegrezza grandissima.
stops.quote_source: Lost letter of Dante on Campaldino, quoted in Leonardo Bruni, Vita di Dante (fragmentary; ellipses mark the joins)
suggested_refs: The Colonna di Dante on the plain of Campaldino, near Certomondo and Poppi
Buonconte da Montefeltro's tear, Purgatorio V

stops.name: Caprona, the surrender of the garrison
stops.campa: Two months after Campaldino, Dante is again under arms, at the siege of the Pisan-Ghibelline fortress of Caprona on the Arno. The garrison, granted safe passage under negotiated terms, files out between two lines of the besieging army; Dante watches men who have just surrendered walk visibly afraid between so many enemies, a sight so exact in his memory that thirty years later he will reach for it as the precise simile for the frightened souls of the barrators emerging from the pitch of Malebolge.
stops.quote: Così vid'io già temer li fanti ch'uscivan patteggiati di Caprona, veggendo sé tra nemici cotanti.
suggested_refs: The ruined Rocca di Caprona above the Arno

stops.name: Florence, matriculation in the guild of physicians and apothecaries
stops.campa: The Ordinances of Justice bar any man without a guild from public office, so on this day Dante enrolls in the Arte dei Medici e Speziali, the guild of doctors, apothecaries, and, not incidentally, booksellers and painters of pigment. He has no trade in medicine; he is buying the one thing Florence will sell a poet for the price of a membership fee, the right to speak in the councils of his own city. Within five years the guild's rolls will carry the name of a prior.
suggested_refs: The guild seat near Orsanmichele, Florence
sources: Arte dei Medici e Speziali matriculation records

stops.name: Florence, the priorate begins
stops.campa: Dante takes his seat among the six Priors of Florence for a term of two months, the highest office the commune gives, in the old Palazzo del Popolo while the new Palazzo is still rising in stone across the piazza. Guelph Florence is tearing itself between Whites and Blacks, Cerchi against Donati, and the priors, Dante among them, judge that the only remedy is to remove both factions' leaders from the city at once. He will call this office, in words his first biographer preserves, the origin and cause of all his misfortunes.
stops.quote: Tutti li mali e tutti gli inconvenienti miei dalli infausti comizi del mio priorato ebbono cagione e principio.
stops.quote_source: Lost letter of Dante, quoted in Leonardo Bruni, Vita di Dante
suggested_refs: The Bargello, seat of Florentine justice

stops.name: Florence, the banishment of Guido Cavalcanti
stops.campa: By the priors' own decree the leaders of both factions are exiled to Sarzana in the fever coast of the Lunigiana, Black and White alike, in the name of civic peace. Among the Whites sent out goes Guido Cavalcanti, the poet Dante calls his first friend, to whom the Vita Nuova itself was dedicated. Guido sickens of the marsh fever within weeks; recalled to Florence by August, he dies of it before the month is out. Dante signs the order that kills the friend who taught him how to write.
suggested_refs: Guido Cavalcanti's sonnets to Dante
Inferno X, Cavalcante de' Cavalcanti's question about his son

stops.name: Rome, the embassy to Boniface VIII
stops.campa: Sent as one of three Florentine envoys to the Lateran to dissuade Pope Boniface VIII from backing Charles of Valois's march into Tuscany, Dante finds the Pope untroubled by the delegation and unwilling to give a plain answer. Boniface, by the account later given, keeps two of the three envoys back in Rome under courteous pretenses, Dante among them, so that time runs against Florence while he talks. Years afterward, from the depth of the eighth circle, Dante will render his verdict on this pope among the simoniacs, upside down in stone, awaiting the day of his own arrival.
stops.quote: Deh, or mi dì: quanto tesoro volle Nostro Segnore in prima da san Pietro ch'ei ponesse le chiavi in sua balìa?
stops.quote_source: Inferno XIX, 90-92 (Dante's later verdict on the simoniac popes)
suggested_refs: The Lateran Palace, papal residence under Boniface VIII

stops.name: Florence, Charles of Valois and the Black coup
stops.campa: Charles of Valois, styled peacemaker by the Pope, rides into Florence with his men-at-arms and stands aside while Corso Donati and the Black Guelphs seize the government by force. For six days the city burns and is looted, White households are sacked, and the courts that survive begin drawing up the charges. Dante, still detained in Rome on the Pope's business, will never again in his life pass through the gates of the city that is, at this hour, being taken from him for good.
suggested_refs: Palazzo Vecchio, seat of the new Black Guelph government

stops.name: Florence, the first sentence in absentia
stops.campa: The podestà Cante de' Gabrielli da Gubbio convicts Dante in absence on charges of barratry, corruption, and opposition to the Pope and to Charles of Valois, fines him five thousand florins he cannot pay, and bars him from office for two years. Dante refuses to appear and answer, knowing an appearance is itself a confession under Black Guelph law. He will spend the rest of his years, in his own words, going as a pilgrim, almost a beggar, through nearly every province where this Italian tongue is spoken, showing against his will the wound that Fortune deals.
stops.quote: per le parti quasi tutte a le quali questa lingua si stende, peregrino, quasi mendicando, sono andato, mostrando contra mia voglia la piaga de la fortuna
suggested_refs: The sentence of 27 January 1302, Archivio di Stato di Firenze
sources: Sentenza del 27 gennaio 1302, Archivio di Stato di Firenze

stops.name: Florence, the second sentence: death by fire
stops.campa: A second decree, harsher than the first, condemns Dante and fourteen others by name to be burned alive should they ever fall into the power of the commune. His sons, once they come of age, will be named in a further decree of the same kind. From this day the sentence is never revoked in his lifetime; the city that made him a poet in her own tongue keeps a fire lit for him, in law, for the remaining nineteen years he has left to live.
suggested_refs: The 10 March 1302 decree, Archivio di Stato di Firenze
sources: Sentenza del 10 marzo 1302, Archivio di Stato di Firenze

stops.name: San Godenzo, the pact of the exiles
stops.campa: In the choir of the Benedictine abbey of San Godenzo, eighteen heads of the exiled White Guelphs and Ghibellines gather and swear a compact, notarized by Giovanni Buto d'Ampinana: to indemnify the Ubaldini counts of the Mugello for any damage the coming war of return does to their castles, in exchange for men and passage. Dante's name stands among the signers, the last time it will ever stand joined to a faction's cause. Within a few years he will break from these same allies and call their whole company wicked and foolish, a party of one from then on.
suggested_refs: The Badia di San Godenzo, Mugello
sources: Paradiso XVII (Cacciaguida's prophecy of the party of one)

stops.name: Forlì, the muster under Scarpetta Ordelaffi
stops.campa: The exiled Whites and their Ghibelline allies gather an army under the Forlì captain Scarpetta Ordelaffi, hoping to fight their way back into Florence. Dante rides among them still, one voice in a council of the disaffected, though he already distrusts the enterprise. The war of return will end in ruinous defeat, at Puliciano in the Mugello and then under Florence's own walls at La Lastra; long before those fields are lost, Dante has begun to draw apart from the company whose folly he will soon condemn outright, in the words of an ancestor not yet spoken to him.
suggested_refs: Scarpetta Ordelaffi's captaincy of the White exiles

stops.name: Verona, the first refuge, Bartolomeo della Scala
stops.campa: Dante finds his first true shelter at the court of Bartolomeo della Scala, lord of Verona, whose house bears the ladder and the eagle on its crest. Here for the first time since Florence a great household feeds and houses him not as a mendicant but as an honored guest, though the bread is another man's bread and the stairs he climbs are another man's stairs. It is a hospitality he will still be praising, and still tasting the bitterness under, when his own ancestor foretells it to him from inside a sphere of fire twelve years hence.
stops.quote: Lo primo tuo refugio e 'l primo ostello sarà la cortesia del gran Lombardo che 'n su la scala porta il santo uccello.
suggested_refs: The della Scala eagle-and-ladder crest, Verona

stops.name: Bologna, the years of study and De Vulgari Eloquentia
stops.campa: Among the schools of Bologna, where he had studied as a young man before the exile, Dante now takes up two ambitious unfinished treatises: the Convivio, a banquet of philosophy set out in the vernacular for those shut out of Latin learning, and the De Vulgari Eloquentia, the first treatise ever written on what makes an Italian vernacular fit for the highest poetry. No one before him, he declares in its opening line, has ever treated the doctrine of eloquence in the vulgar tongue. He is still building, in exile, the very language his sentence was written in.
stops.quote: Cum neminem ante nos de vulgaris eloquentiae doctrina quicquam inveniamus tractasse...
suggested_refs: The University of Bologna's medieval schools

stops.name: Lunigiana, the Malaspina court and the Peace of Castelnuovo
stops.campa: Taken in by the Malaspina marquises, Dante repays their courtesy in the coin he has: on this morning in the piazza of Castelnuovo Magra, Marquis Franceschino Malaspina names him executor, procurator, and special ambassador with full power to conclude, on the whole Ghibelline branch's behalf, a peace with Antonio Nuvolone da Camilla, bishop-count of Luni, ending a long and bitter feud over the Lunigiana valleys. The exile who cannot enter his own city as a private man signs a treaty between a marquis and a bishop as a plenipotentiary.
suggested_refs: The bishop's castle at Castelnuovo Magra
Purgatorio VIII, Currado Malaspina's praise of his house
sources: Atto della Pace di Castelnuovo, 6 ottobre 1306, Archivio di Stato della Spezia

stops.name: Casentino, Poppi Castle and the canto of Ugolino
stops.campa: At Poppi, guest of Count Guido da Battifolle and his countess Gherardesca, Dante writes three Latin letters in her name to the Empress Margherita of Brabant. Gherardesca is the daughter of Count Ugolino della Gherardesca of Pisa, starved to death with his sons and grandsons in the Tower of Hunger for an alleged betrayal; inside these same castle walls, under this same roof, Dante composes the canto that gives Ugolino's ravenous ghost, gnawing the skull of the archbishop who caged him, its final and most terrible line.
stops.quote: Poscia, più che 'l dolor, poté 'l digiuno.
suggested_refs: The Castello dei Conti Guidi, Poppi
Inferno XXXIII, Ugolino in the Tower of Hunger
sources: Epistole di Dante, in nome di Gherardesca da Battifolle

stops.name: Lucca, refuge and Gentucca
stops.campa: Somewhere among the cities of his wandering Dante passes months at Lucca, sheltered, tradition says, in the house of Gentucca Morla; the shade of the poet Bonagiunta Orbicciani will greet him in Purgatory itself with news of an unwed Lucchese woman who will yet make that city please him, and asks whether he is truly the one who drew forth the new rhymes beginning with the words about women who have understanding of love. Dante answers that he is only a scribe, taking down what Love itself dictates within him.
stops.quote: Ma dì s'i' veggio qui colui che fore trasse le nove rime, cominciando 'Donne ch'avete intelletto d'amore'.
suggested_refs: The traditional house of Gentucca, Lucca

stops.name: Verona, the court of Cangrande della Scala
stops.campa: Dante returns to Verona, now ruled by Bartolomeo's younger brother Cangrande, the Great Dog, imperial vicar, the most magnificent lord in Lombardy and the most generous host of Dante's whole exile. Here he is given not charity but honor, a household of his own within the household, years of settled work on the Paradiso. His ancestor Cacciaguida, still unspoken to him at this point of the story but already speaking of it from Mars, foretells that this young lord, born under a strong star, will do deeds his enemies will not be able to keep silent about, however they try.
stops.quote: Con lui vedrai colui che 'mpresso fue, nascendo, sì da questa stella forte, che notabili fier l'opere sue.
suggested_refs: Cangrande della Scala's equestrian tomb monument, Verona

stops.name: Verona, the Epistle to Cangrande
stops.campa: In a long Latin letter of dedication, Dante gives his protector, and the ages after him, the only key to the Commedia's meaning that its own author will ever set down in plain prose: that the poem is polysemous, carrying more than one sense at once, literal and allegorical together, and that its whole aim, and the aim of every part of it, is to lead those living this present life out of the state of misery and into the state of felicity. He dedicates the Paradiso, canticle by canticle, to the lord under whose roof he writes it.
stops.quote: finis totius et partis est removere viventes in hac vita de statu miserie et perducere ad statum felicitatis
stops.quote_source: Epistola XIII, to Cangrande della Scala, §39 (authorship debated by some scholars)
suggested_refs: Manuscript tradition of the Epistola XIII

stops.name: Verona, the Quaestio de aqua et terra
stops.campa: Before the assembled clergy and learned men of Verona, in the church of Sant'Elena beside the cathedral, Dante reads a formal scholastic disputation on a question much argued in the schools: whether water, anywhere on the globe, rises higher than the dry land, even at the antipodes. He answers no, and defends it point by point against the philosophers, the very same cosmography by which, in his poem, the mountain of Purgatory stands alone out of the southern ocean, the one dry land raised up on the far side of the world from Jerusalem.
suggested_refs: Chiesa di Santa Elena, Verona, beside the Duomo
sources: Dante, Quaestio de aqua et terra, 20 gennaio 1320

segments.name: Ravenna: the Paradiso Finished and the Death

stops.name: Ravenna, the court of Guido Novello da Polenta
stops.campa: Guido Novello da Polenta, lord of Ravenna and nephew of Francesca, whose own doomed love Dante had set among the lustful years before, invites the poet to his court on the Adriatic marshes. Here at last, after sixteen years of other men's stairs, Dante is given a settled house, honor, and the company of his sons Jacopo and Pietro and his daughter Antonia, who will one day take the veil under the name Sister Beatrice. It is the nearest thing to a home he will have again, and it is where he means to finish the third canticle.
suggested_refs: The da Polenta seal, a golden eagle
sources: Boccaccio, Trattatello in laude di Dante

stops.name: Ravenna, the eclogues to Giovanni del Virgilio
stops.campa: From Bologna the humanist Giovanni del Virgilio writes urging Dante to abandon the vernacular and win true, lasting fame by composing in Latin instead, the tongue of Virgil and of scholars. Dante answers not with an argument but with a pair of Latin pastoral eclogues, in the manner of Virgil's own, declining the invitation to Bologna and defending, in the classical form del Virgilio himself prizes, his choice to finish his great poem in the speech of ordinary Italians.
suggested_refs: Dante's Latin Eclogues, in reply to Giovanni del Virgilio

stops.name: Ravenna, the Paradiso finished
stops.campa: The last cantos of the Paradiso are completed, closing a poem begun some twenty years before in a dark wood and carried across three courts and half of Italy. Boccaccio will later record a marvel about their ending: that after Dante's death his sons could find no trace of the final thirteen cantos, until Jacopo, visited in a dream by his father's shade, is led to a wall recess hidden behind a straw mat, where the missing pages, safe from damp and mice, are found exactly as the poem needed them.
suggested_refs: Boccaccio's account of the hidden final cantos
sources: Boccaccio, Trattatello in laude di Dante

stops.name: Venice, the embassy for Guido Novello
stops.campa: Guido Novello, in dispute with Venice over the salt trade and galley incursions along the Adriatic coast, sends Dante as his ambassador to treat with the Doge. The Signoria receives him coolly and grants little; Dante begins the return journey by the lagoon roads through the fever marshes of Comacchio, where the summer air carries the malaria that has already killed Guido Cavalcanti and Ugolino's own line. He does not know, riding home, that he is carrying his own death in his blood.
suggested_refs: The Doge's palace, Venice, receiving Ravenna's embassy
sources: Boccaccio, Trattatello in laude di Dante

stops.name: Ravenna, the death
stops.campa: The fever taken at Comacchio does not break. In the night between the thirteenth and fourteenth of September, in the house of Guido Novello, with the completed hundred cantos of his poem finished and safe, Dante Alighieri dies at fifty-six. No last words of his are recorded. Boccaccio writes only that he trusts the poet's noblest soul was received, at that hour, into the arms of his own Beatrice, in the country where the pilgrim of thirty cantos had already told everyone he was going.
suggested_refs: Boccaccio's account of Dante's death, September 1321
sources: Boccaccio, Trattatello in laude di Dante

stops.name: Ravenna, burial at San Pier Maggiore
stops.campa: Guido Novello buries Dante with full public honor at the church of San Pier Maggiore, later renamed San Francesco, in a marble tomb by the city wall, and reportedly means to raise a much grander monument that his own fall from power the next year prevents. An epitaph in Latin elegiacs, traditionally held to be of Dante's own drafting, is later carved over him: the laws of monarchy, the heavens, Phlegethon and the lakes of the underworld, he sang, as far as the fates allowed. Florence, which condemned him to burn, will spend seven centuries asking for his bones back; Ravenna has never given them up.
stops.quote: Iura monarchiae, superos, Phlegetonta, lacusque lustrando cecini, voluerunt fata quousque.
stops.quote_source: Epitaph traditionally ascribed to Dante himself, inscribed by Bernardo Bembo, 1483
suggested_refs: The Tomba di Dante, Ravenna, rebuilt 1780-81
The Zona Dantesca and the perpetual lamp fed with Florentine oil
sources: Tomb inscription, Zona del Sepolcro di Dante, Ravenna
Boccaccio, Trattatello in laude di Dante

stops.name: The dark wood, in the middle of life's road
stops.campa: Midway upon the journey of our life, Dante finds himself lost in a dark wood, the straight way gone. No commentator has ever fixed a real place to this wood; it is nowhere and every reader's own life at once. He tries to climb a sunlit hill and is turned back by a leopard, a lion, and a she-wolf, until a shade appears who names himself: Virgil, sent by three blessed ladies in Heaven, Mary, Lucy, and Beatrice herself, to lead him by a longer road, through Hell and up the mountain, back toward the light.
stops.quote: Nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita mi ritrovai per una selva oscura, ché la diritta via era smarrita.
suggested_refs: Gustave Doré's engraving of the dark wood and the three beasts
Botticelli's map of Hell

stops.name: The Gate of Hell, beneath the world
stops.campa: Virgil leads him to a gate inscribed in dark letters above its arch, warning that through it lies the city of woe, eternal pain, the lost people, and that all hope must be left behind by whoever enters. This gate opens the funnel of Hell that plunges, in the poem's own cosmology, straight down beneath the northern hemisphere to the center of the earth, its point falling directly under the hill of Jerusalem where Christ was crucified, and antipodal, on the far side of that same axis, to the mountain later to be climbed.
stops.quote: Per me si va ne la città dolente, per me si va ne l'etterno dolore... Lasciate ogne speranza, voi ch'intrate.
suggested_refs: The lettered gate of Hell, illustrated across centuries of manuscripts
sources: Purgatorio II and Inferno XXXIV (the cosmology of Hell beneath Jerusalem)

stops.name: Limbo, the noble castle of the unbaptized wise
stops.campa: In the first circle, sorrowless but without hope, Dante finds a lit castle ringed by seven walls holding the great pre-Christian and unbaptized souls: Homer, Horace, Ovid, Lucan, who make Dante a sixth among their company, and, seated apart in a philosophical family with Socrates and Plato nearest him, the master of those who know: Aristotle, whom every philosophy in the castle honors and reveres. Here too stands Virgil's own eternal home, the guide who must lead Dante everywhere but through the gate at the very top of the mountain still far ahead.
stops.quote: vidi 'l maestro di color che sanno seder tra filosofica famiglia.
suggested_refs: Raphael's School of Athens, echoing this same philosophical company
aristotle.journey.json — the master of those who know, before Limbo held him
plato.journey.json — seated nearest him in the same philosophical family

stops.name: The circle of Lust, Paolo and Francesca
stops.campa: In the storm of the second circle, blown forever together, Francesca da Rimini tells Dante how she and her husband's brother Paolo, reading together one day of Lancelot and Guinevere for pleasure alone, came to the page where the fictional lovers kissed, and read no further that day. Love, she says, which absolves no one beloved from loving back, seized her for Paolo's beauty so strongly that it has not left her even here. Dante, hearing her, is so overcome with pity that he falls to the ground as a dead body falls.
stops.quote: Amor, ch'a nullo amato amar perdona, mi prese del costui piacer sì forte, che, come vedi, ancor non m'abbandona.
suggested_refs: Ary Scheffer's and Rodin's renderings of Paolo and Francesca

stops.name: The City of Dis, Farinata degli Uberti
stops.campa: Past the walls of the burning city of Dis, among the heretics in open flaming tombs, the Ghibelline captain Farinata degli Uberti rises from his own sepulcher from the waist up, as though he held all of Hell in contempt, to demand who Dante's ancestors were, recognizing at once an old Guelph enemy's blood. From inside the same tomb Cavalcante de' Cavalcanti, father of Dante's own dead friend Guido, rears up beside him, desperate to know whether his son still lives. Farinata, unmoved, returns to prophesying Dante's own coming exile, which he already knows from his vantage on time itself.
stops.quote: ed el s'ergea col petto e con la fronte com'avesse l'inferno a gran dispitto.
suggested_refs: The tombs of the heresiarchs, City of Dis

stops.name: The circle of Fraud, the last voyage of Ulysses
stops.campa: Wrapped in a single horned flame among the false counselors, Ulysses, unknown to Homer's own Mediterranean, tells Dante of a last voyage never sung before: how, old and restless even after his return to Ithaca, he gathered his aged crew and sailed them past the Pillars of Hercules, out into the forbidden ocean, urging them on with the argument that they were not made to live like brutes but to follow virtue and knowledge, until a mountain rose from the sea, and a whirlwind span the ship three times and sank it, as pleased Another.
stops.quote: Considerate la vostra semenza: fatti non foste a viver come bruti, ma per seguir virtute e canoscenza.
suggested_refs: Tennyson's Ulysses, descended directly from this canto
ulysses.journey.json — the same mariner's own epic homeward voyage, ending instead at Ithaca

stops.name: Cocytus, Ugolino and Lucifer at the world's center
stops.campa: Frozen in the ice of Cocytus, Count Ugolino gnaws eternally at the skull of Archbishop Ruggieri, who walled him and his sons and grandsons into the Tower of Hunger to starve; he tells Dante the whole pity of it, ending only in the silence of hunger doing what grief could not. Deeper still, at the exact center of the earth and of the universe, the three-faced Lucifer stands waist-deep in ice, battering the air with six vast bat-wings whose wind is the very cold that freezes the lake around him, gnawing Judas, Brutus, and Cassius in his three mouths. Climbing down his shaggy flank past the earth's midpoint, Virgil and Dante find themselves, without turning, suddenly climbing up.
stops.quote: Vexilla regis prodeunt inferni verso di noi; però dinanzi mira, disse 'l maestro mio, se tu 'l discerni.
suggested_refs: Doré's Lucifer at the center of the ice
The Tower of Hunger, Pisa

segments.name: The Mountain of Purgatory and the Flight to the Empyrean

stops.name: The shore of Purgatory, Cato
stops.campa: Climbing up through a natural tunnel from the earth's center, Dante and Virgil emerge before dawn on Easter Sunday onto the shore of an island mountain rising alone from a southern ocean, directly antipodal to Jerusalem, the one dry land the earth recoiled to make when Lucifer fell and buried himself at the opposite pole. Its guardian is Cato of Utica, pagan and suicide yet set here in freedom's honor, who challenges the newcomers sharply before Virgil answers him and Dante is girded with a reed at the shore, the humility that Purgatory alone requires.
stops.quote: Chi siete voi che contro al cieco fiume fuggita avete la pregione etterna?
suggested_refs: The traditional antipodal geography: Purgatory's mountain opposite Jerusalem

stops.name: Ante-purgatory, the song of Casella
stops.campa: On the lower slope, among souls who died reconciled to God but late, Dante meets his old friend the musician Casella, freshly landed from the boat of souls an angel ferries across from the mouth of the Tiber. Asked for comfort, Casella sings one of Dante's own philosophical canzoni, Love that discourses to me in my mind, so sweetly that the whole crowd of souls stands rapt and motionless, until Cato comes storming up the slope rebuking the delay: souls with a mountain to climb have no business lingering over songs.
stops.quote: Amor che ne la mente mi ragiona
suggested_refs: Dante's own canzone, set by later composers
The angel-boat ferrying souls from the Tiber's mouth

stops.name: The Gate of Peter, the seven wounds
stops.campa: At the true gate of Purgatory proper, an angel seated on a diamond threshold above three steps, white marble, black and cracked, and blood-red porphyry, draws the point of his sword seven times across Dante's forehead, cutting seven P's, for peccata, for the seven capital sins, telling him to see that he washes these wounds away once inside. Each terrace he climbs will lift one letter from his brow, until he reaches the top light as the last one falls away.
stops.quote: Sette P ne la fronte mi descrisse col punton de la spada, e 'Fa che lavi, quando se' dentro, queste piaghe' disse.
suggested_refs: The three-stepped threshold of Purgatory's gate, white, black, and porphyry-red

stops.name: The terraces, from pride to the wall of fire
stops.campa: Ring by ring Dante climbs the seven terraces where pride, envy, wrath, sloth, avarice, gluttony, and lust are scoured away, each with its own carved examples of virtue and whip of vice, its own beatitude sung at the passage upward. On the last terrace the poet Guido Guinizzelli points out an even greater craftsman of love poetry ahead of him in the flame, the Provençal troubadour Arnaut Daniel, who answers Dante's courteous question in his own southern tongue before diving back into the refining fire that every soul here must pass through to reach the top.
stops.quote: Tan m'abellis vostre cortes deman, qu'ieu no me puesc ni voill a vos cobrire.
suggested_refs: Ezra Pound's translations of Arnaut Daniel, drawn from this canto

stops.name: The Earthly Paradise, the return of Beatrice
stops.campa: At the summit, in the garden of Eden itself, a pageant of the Church triumphant approaches through the wood, and within it, veiled in white and crowned with olive over a green mantle and a flame-red dress, stands Beatrice, dead now ten years, alive in this place forever. Virgil, having led Dante through every circle of Hell and up every terrace of the mountain, has vanished without a word, his pagan office ended at the gate of grace; Dante turns to tell him so and finds him gone, and it is Beatrice, calling him by name for the only time in the whole poem, who takes his soul in hand from here.
stops.quote: Guardaci ben! Ben son, ben son Beatrice.
suggested_refs: The pageant of the griffin and the chariot, Purgatorio XXIX
Virgil's silent disappearance, Purgatorio XXX

stops.name: The sphere of Mars, Cacciaguida's prophecy of exile
stops.campa: Carried by Beatrice up through the Moon, Mercury, Venus, and the Sun, where Aquinas and Bonaventure circle him in rings of light, Dante rises into the red sphere of Mars, shaped like a cross of souls, and there meets his own great-great-grandfather Cacciaguida, a crusader knight who greets him in Latin as blood of his blood. Cacciaguida tells him plainly, for the first time in the whole poem stated outright rather than only glimpsed, what is coming: exile from Florence, the bitterness of another man's bread and another man's stairs, and the sorrow of standing alone, a party unto himself.
stops.quote: tu proverai sì come sa di sale lo pane altrui, e come è duro calle lo scendere e 'l salir per l'altrui scale.
suggested_refs: Cacciaguida's Latin greeting, Paradiso XV: O sanguis meus

stops.name: The sphere of the Fixed Stars, looking back at the earth
stops.campa: In the eighth heaven, among the fixed stars beneath the constellation of his own birth, Dante is examined in turn by Saint Peter on faith, Saint James on hope, and Saint John on love, three questionings he answers well enough to be told he has passed. Before ascending further he is told to look down, and through all seven spheres he has climbed he sees the whole small circuit of the earth below him, the little threshing-floor that makes men so fierce over so little ground, and he smiles at the pettiness of it from that height.
stops.quote: l'aiuola che ci fa tanto feroci
suggested_refs: The Earthrise photograph, echoing the same vantage of smallness

stops.name: The Empyrean, the celestial rose and the vision of God
stops.campa: Past the crystalline Primum Mobile, outside space and time, Dante and Beatrice arrive at the Empyrean, pure light, where the blessed sit tiered in the petals of an enormous white rose and Saint Bernard, taking Beatrice's place as final guide, prays to the Virgin for grace to look, one instant, directly at God. Dante's sight, strengthened past its own nature, sees within the eternal light three circles of three colors bound into one, our human image seeming to fit within the second; his own power fails at the height of it, but his will is already turned, like a wheel moved evenly, by the same force that moves the sun and the other stars.
stops.quote: l'amor che move il sole e l'altre stelle.
suggested_refs: The celestial rose, illustrated by Gustave Doré
Botticelli's drawings for the Paradiso
